title:
Demon Slayer, Street Fighter and Shield Hero Voice Actor, Stephen Fu Celebrates 41! 🎙️🔥🎮

Stephen Fu has quickly become
title_en:
Demon Slayer, Street Fighter and Shield Hero Voice Actor, Stephen Fu Celebrates 41! 🎙️🔥🎮

Stephen Fu has quickly become a familiar voice across modern anime and gaming, bringing a striking range of heroes, villains, and fan favorites to life. His chilling performance as Douma in Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba stands alongside major game roles like Iron Fist / Lin Lie in Marvel Rivals, Jamie in Street Fighter 6, and Hwei in League of Legends.

Anime fans also know him as Naofumi Iwatani in The Rising of the Shield Hero, Weather Report in JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: Stone Ocean, Sakuta Azusagawa in Rascal Does Not Dream of Bunny Girl Senpai, and Lance Crown in Mashle: Magic and Muscles. Newer roles such as Anaxa in Honkai: Star Rail, Natsuki Seba in Sakamoto Days, and Naito Mudano in Tougen Anki continue to expand an already impressive résumé.

Some of his most notable voice roles include:
• Douma — Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba
• Iron Fist / Lin Lie — Marvel Rivals
• Jamie — Street Fighter 6
• Cho Sang-woo — Squid Game
• Naofumi Iwatani — The Rising of the Shield Hero
• Hwei — League of Legends
• Wise — Zenless Zone Zero
• Weather Report — JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: Stone Ocean
• Sakuta Azusagawa — Rascal Does Not Dream of Bunny Girl Senpai
• Anaxa — Honkai: Star Rail
• Lance Crown — Mashle: Magic and Muscles
• Henry Legolant — Black Clover
• Seiji Shishikura — My Hero Academia
• Ryo Saeba — City Hunter
• Noé Archiviste — The Case Study of Vanitas
• Shinpei Ajiro — Summer Time Rendering
• Akito Yamada — My Love Story with Yamada-kun at Lv999
• Natsuki Seba — Sakamoto Days
• Naito Mudano — Tougen Anki
• Khrome Ryugu — Beyblade X

With roles spanning intense villains, laid-back leads, fighters, and emotionally complex heroes, Fu continues to make his mark across some of anime and gaming’s biggest worlds.

Happy 41st Birthday, Stephen Fu! 🎂✨

full_text_zh:
鬼灭之刃、街头霸王、盾牌英雄配音演员傅士芬庆祝 41 岁生日！ 🎙️🔥🎮

史蒂芬·傅 (Stephen Fu) 迅速成为现代动漫和游戏领域的知名人物，将一系列引人注目的英雄、反派和粉丝最爱的角色带入生活。他在《鬼灭之刃》中饰演 Douma 的令人毛骨悚然的表演，与《漫威对手》中的铁拳 / 林烈、《街头霸王 6》中的 Jamie 以及《英雄联盟》中的 Hwei 等主要游戏角色齐名。

动漫迷们还知道他在《盾之勇者成名录》中扮演岩谷尚文、在《JoJo的奇妙冒险：石之海》中扮演天气预报、在《青春猪头少年不会梦到兔女郎学姐》中的梓川咲太以及在《魔法与肌肉》中扮演兰斯·克朗。新角色，如《崩坏：星轨》中的阿那克萨、《坂本时代》中的濑叶夏希以及《桃源 Anki》中的内藤·穆达诺，继续扩大本已令人印象深刻的履历。

他的一些最著名的配音角色包括：
• Douma — 鬼灭之刃：Kimetsu no Yaiba
• 铁拳 / 林烈 — Marvel Rivals
• 杰米 — 街头霸王 6
• Cho Sang-woo — 鱿鱼游戏
• 岩谷尚文 — 《盾之勇者成名录》
• Hwei — 英雄联盟
• Wise — Zenless 零区
• 天气预报 — JoJo的奇妙冒险：石之海
• 梓川咲太 — 青春猪头少年不会梦到兔女郎学姐
• Anaxa — 崩坏：星轨
• Lance Crown — Mashle：魔法与肌肉
• 亨利·莱戈兰特——《黑色四叶草》
• 狮子仓精二 — 我的英雄学院
• Ryo Saeba — 城市猎人
• Noé Archiviste — Vanitas 案例研究
• Shinpei Ajiro — 夏季渲染
• Akito Yamada — 我与山田君的爱情故事 Lv999
• 濑场夏希 — 坂本时代
• 内藤·穆达诺 — Tougen Anki
• Khrome Ryugu — Beyblade X

傅的角色涵盖激烈的反派、悠闲的主角、战士和情感复杂的英雄，他继续在动漫和游戏的一些最大的世界中留下自己的印记。

傅士芬 41 岁生日快乐！ 🎂✨

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 百度官方宣布文心大模型ERNIE 5.5 Flash预览版现已通过vLLM-ERNIE插件获得vLLM框架的即时（Day-0）支持。该模型采用280B总参数量与14B激活参数的混合专家（MoE）架构，具备推理与工具调用能力，并支持高达100万token的长文本上下文处理。

elements_en.what: Launched vLLM-ERNIE plugin for ERNIE 5.5 Flash, enabling 1M token context
elements_en.why: To improve deployment performance and ecosystem compatibility via open-source inference standards

ai_analysis.insight_zh: ERNIE系列通过接入vLLM插件，实质上是百度在开源推理基础设施层面的生态卡位，旨在降低开发者在其MoE模型上的落地门槛。此举不仅是对抗同类长上下文模型竞争的差异化策略，更是通过与主流推理框架的深度绑定，加速其模型在私有化部署市场的份额渗透。
ai_analysis.insight_en: By integrating with the vLLM plugin, Baidu is strategically securing its position within the open-source inference ecosystem to lower barriers for MoE model deployment. This move serves as a competitive play against other long-context models, aiming to accelerate market penetration in private deployment by aligning with standardized inference infrastructures.

title:
He's right.  We are experiencing the death of thought.

Just now, I had to read a hefty AI-generated 900-word post about
title_en:
He's right.  We are experiencing the death of thought.

Just now, I had to read a hefty AI-generated 900-word post about a guy who printed a contract and used a mechanical pencil.

Rather than skim it for 12 seconds, whisper “good for him,” and move on with my evening, I did something radical.

I didn’t print your post on a Wi-Fi laser printer like some kind of Silicon Valley soft-hands.

I transcribed every single one of your 902 words by hand onto unbleached calfskin vellum using a goose quill I cured in my own garage, sharpened it with a dull pocketknife until my thumb bled, and spent four and a half hours marking up the margins in homemade iron-gall ink.

I finished writing down my thoughts in the margins, set down my quill, stared silently at a brass lamp, and reflected on what just happened.

I felt deeply satisfied, wildly embarrassed, mildly dehydrated, and somehow taller all at once.

I couldn’t remember the last time I had used my brain for an end-to-end process without relying on an industrial convenience like a mechanical pencil or Hewlett-Packard toner. I felt total command over your post. I felt crystalline clarity about what I understood, what I didn’t understand, and why a grown man felt moved to alert the entire timeline that he had read a PDF with a pencil. And I was left with unshakable conviction in my POV.

Moreover, I felt the high of “ultra-clean” dopamine.

Not the factory-farmed, seed-oil dopamine you get from pressing a plastic thumb-clicker on a 0.7mm Pentel like a lab rat tapping a lever for pellets. Not the lukewarm, ultra-processed dopamine of reading a contract printed out on bleached 20-pound copy paper that a machine collated for you without even asking you to set the movable type.

No. I’m talking about single-origin, cold-pressed, pasture-raised dopamine. The kind of raw, unadulterated neurochemical high our ancestors felt when they sat down at a mahogany desk, read an actual contract from page one to the signature block, and didn’t immediately open LinkedIn to announce that they had survived the ordeal.

Then I felt embarrassed.

How long had I been depriving myself of turning basic adult errands into sweeping civilizational manifestos?

Just yesterday, I made two slices of sourdough toast without once asking Claude to “review this loaf, break down the crumb structure, and give me feedback as if you’re my baker.” I stood there in front of the toaster like a pioneer on the Oregon Trail, watched the heating coils glow orange, buttered the bread manually, and ate it. And what did I do afterward? Nothing. I just rinsed my plate and went to work. Not a single 1,000-word reflection on the erosion of culinary agency. Not one mention of Socrates. Not one bulleted list of ways to reclaim the sacred space between bread and butter.

I was disgusted with myself.

And then I got curious.

In fact, I got so curious that I had to sit down, because curiosity at this altitude can make a man lightheaded.

Why is it that every time somebody in tech rediscovers an office supply from 1987, he feels spiritually compelled to summon Daniel Kahneman, Socrates, and Viktor Frankl like the Avengers? And what can we do to make sure we don’t surrender our last remaining shred of self-awareness to the Thought Leadership Industrial Complex?

The answer lies in what Daniel Kahneman called System 1 and System 2 thinking, and more importantly, in the three higher systems that Kahneman was too polite to put in the book.

Everyone on the internet loves citing System 1 and System 2, mostly because Thinking, Fast and Slow is the single most-referenced book among people who read a four-page summary of it in 2016 and have been dining out on the phrase “lazy controller” ever since.

System 1 is fast, automatic, and gut-driven thought. It’s what fires when a 42-page commercial agreement lands in your inbox on a Thursday afternoon and your brain immediately says, “I am not reading all of this, I should probably pay an actual lawyer instead of asking a chatbot to roleplay as one.”

System 2 is deliberate, analytical, effortful, and conscious. It’s what fires when you ignore System 1, print the 42-page agreement yourself, grab a mechanical pencil, write “check indemnity??” and “what does mutatis mutandis mean” in the margins for 90 minutes, and walk away from your desk feeling like John Marshall presiding over Marbury v. Madison.

But stopping at System 2 is rookie-level cognition. If you really want to diagnose what is happening to the human mind in 2026, you have to go deeper:

System 3 is performing System 2 in public so strangers know you still have a prefrontal cortex. You didn’t merely read the contract. You observed yourself reading the contract from a cinematic third-person camera angle, felt a single noble tear roll down your cheek, and started mentally workshopping the opening hook somewhere around Section 7.2(b).

System 4 is taking a completely normal Tuesday afternoon task (reading a document before you sign it) and laundering it through one ancient Greek philosopher, three cognitive psychologists, a misattributed quote, ten repetitive bullet points, and a closing comparison to the sun until a routine administrative chore sounds like the drafting of the Magna Carta.

System 5 is reading someone else’s System 4 post and concluding that the only proportionate moral response is to construct an even longer, even more grandiose System 4 post, thereby testing the structural load limits of the X Premium character counter and everybody’s patience simultaneously.

Technology has been hijacking effortful thinking for far longer than 370 BC. Frankly, starting the timeline with Socrates is System 1 history.

Roughly a million years ago: Fire hijacked raw-meat mastication as a gastrointestinal System 2 exercise. Early hominids no longer had to chew elk cartilage for four uninterrupted hours just to extract 300 calories. Immediate metabolic offloading. Everything went downhill from there.

3200 BC: Sumerian cuneiform hijacked remembering how many goats your brother-in-law owed you from the spring harvest. Within two generations, nobody could keep track of a single goat in their head. Pure cognitive atrophy.

1440 AD: Gutenberg’s printing press hijacked the deeply satisfying, hard-fought labor of being a medieval monk squinting in an unheated stone scriptorium for eleven years to hand-copy one manuscript by tallow candle. Did anyone pause to ask what the printing press was doing to the monks’ taste?

1784: Bifocals hijacked squinting as an ocular System 2 exercise.

1822: John Isaac Hawkins and Sampson Mordan secured British Patent No. 4742 for the first mechanical pencil, explicitly designed in the words of the patent itself for “rendering the frequent cutting or mending of the points or nibs unnecessary.”

Stop and sit with that for a moment.

The very mechanical pencil you held aloft yesterday as your Excalibur against Silicon Valley is itself a 204-year-old machine engineered to offload the noble, character-building friction of whittling cedarwood with a blade and blowing graphite dust off your thumb. You didn’t reject shortcuts. You just picked a Victorian shortcut and called it enlightenment.

1959: The Xerox 914 photocopier hijacked retyping contracts on carbon paper.

1983: Microsoft Word hijacked Wite-Out and the healthy, adrenaline-soaked terror of making a typo on page 14 of a 15-page lease.

Calculators hijacked long division.
GPS hijacked arguing with your spouse over a folded Rand McNally road atlas on the center console while missing the exit for Savannah.
Google hijacked sitting at a bar for three hours insisting to your friends that Kevin Costner was in Air Force One when it was actually Harrison Ford, the kind of hard-fought, unadulterated barstool conviction that used to build real character.

Now, to be completely fair to you, you’re right about one big thing. AI really is different.

It doesn’t just take over one effortful job at a time. It takes over all of them at once.

Remembering. Summarizing. Researching. Calculating. Writing. Problem-solving. Weighing trade-offs. Deciding. Planning. Navigating people. Reflecting. Creating. Sounding like a 2019 Medium post. Putting “&” instead of “and” ten times inside a 5,300-character essay where nobody was running out of space. Using the verb “grok” unironically in a manifesto about resisting the machines. Building a ten-item bulleted list where four of the bullets are literally the same bullet wearing different sweaters.

For 200,000 years, our brains have been wired to take the easy out. And when we surrender to shortcuts, whether it’s letting an LLM read our contracts or letting LinkedIn formatting do the heavy lifting of sounding profound, we pay a steep price.

Let’s break down the real costs.

Cost 1: A summary feels like understanding, and a numbered framework feels like wisdom.

You’re completely right that reading a compressed summary tricks your brain into believing you understand a subject you never actually wrestled with. What gets overlooked is the mirror-image trap: taking a twelve-word piece of common sense (“If you don’t read the contract, you won’t know what’s in it”) and inflating it into a 900-word lecture about Paleolithic brain evolution tricks both the author and the reader into thinking they just witnessed a breakthrough in epistemology. Packaging isn’t insight. Single-line paragraphs aren’t depth.

Like this.

And this.

Notice how your brain wants to nod slowly right now, even though I haven’t said anything since the previous paragraph. That’s System 1 getting played by line breaks.

Cost 2: The messy middle is the space for growth, which is also where you discover that reviewing a hefty contract without a lawyer is an exciting way to buy a lawsuit.

Robert Bjork’s work on “desirable difficulties” at UCLA is genuinely great research, and Risko and Gilbert’s work on cognitive offloading is real too. Effortful retrieval makes learning stick. Nobody serious disagrees with that. The funny part is acting like desirable difficulty is an endangered species we have to artificially manufacture with “no-AI blocks,” as if real life isn’t already handing out nine hours of involuntary desirable difficulty every single weekday. Try closing a deal with a stubborn lender, managing a payroll when receivables slip, or reading Section 14.3(c) of a commercial lease where the other side quietly buried a personal guaranty inside a boilerplate maintenance clause. You don’t need a 10-minute productivity hack to experience cognitive friction. Just have actual skin in the game.

Cost 3: The disappearance of judgement, and the rise of the performative sigh.

You asked what will stay uniquely human as we approach AGI and ASI, and you gave us four pillars:

1. Intent
2. Accountability
3. Relationships
4. Judgement

Solid start. Respectable list. A little short, though. If we’re being honest about the final frontier of human uniqueness in the age of superintelligence, there are at least six more traits no neural network will ever truly replicate:

5. Printing a 30-page PDF so you can carry it around the house looking burdened and important.
6. Telling everybody at dinner that you’ve “been going really analog lately.”
7. Buying a $65 brass mechanical pencil from a specialty stationery shop in Kyoto so your margin notes have better mouthfeel.
8. Calling regular job satisfaction “clean dopamine” because saying “I felt good about finishing my work” doesn’t sound like a Huberman episode.
9. Assuming that because you used to outsource your thinking to Claude, the rest of Western civilization forgot how to read a document.
10. Confusing “having taste” with “posting about how important taste is.”

Taste really is thousands of compressed System 2 patterns firing at once. You know what one of those patterns looks like? Reading your own draft back before hitting Post and thinking, “Wait, did I really just compare myself reading a contract with a pencil to fighting for the survival of human thought?”

Cost 4: The Viktor Frankl Industrial Complex.

Every serious productivity essay on the internet must, by federal statute, include the exact quote:

“Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom.”

It’s a lovely sentiment. There is just one tiny, delicious wrinkle.

Viktor Frankl never wrote it.

Researchers have searched Man’s Search for Meaning and the rest of Frankl’s published works top to bottom. Those words aren’t there. Stephen Covey popularized the line after coming across a similar passage in a university library book in Hawaii (scholars point to psychologist Rollo May’s 1963 writing on pausing between stimulus and response as the closest precursor), and somewhere around the mid-2000s the internet glued Viktor Frankl’s name onto it and never looked back.

Think about the sheer poetry of that. A few lines above your own bullet point commanding humanity to “Read the full source, not the summary,” you dropped the single most famous misattributed summary-culture quote on the entire internet.

If that isn’t a case study in cognitive offloading, nothing is.

Cost 5: The hyperinflation of metaphors.

Once upon a time, a contract was a contract and the sun was a 4.6-billion-year-old ball of fusing hydrogen plasma 93 million miles from Earth that grows crops, powers the water cycle, and gives you a leathery neck if you skip sunscreen on the back nine.

Now a probabilistic text engine that tells you “That’s a really sharp, nuanced point!” every time you misspell a question is “like the sun.”

If AI is the sun, what does that make the mechanical pencil? A patio umbrella? SPF 50? A pair of polarized sunglasses? Once you start comparing software subscriptions to nuclear fusion in space, you leave yourself nowhere to go when something actually important happens.

Cost 6: The collapse of proportionality.

When every minor personal realization (today I read a document carefully instead of skimming an AI bullet list!) has to be framed as an existential battle at the edge of the species, our collective sense of scale breaks down. Sometimes you didn’t strike a blow against the death of thought. Sometimes you just did your homework.

So how do we take back our thinking, our brevity, and our dignity, while still embracing this transformative technology?

It resolves down to one key principle: rebuild the space between having a normal afternoon and writing a 900-word sermon about it.

How you rebuild that space is completely up to you. Pick your poison:

- Create 30-to-60-minute no-AI blocks in your day, followed immediately by 90-minute no-posting blocks so you don’t undo the entire spiritual benefit by bragging about it online.
- Go analog and print out what matters. Then print out something that doesn’t matter at all, just to maintain dominance over your printer.
- Ditch the mechanical pencil. Use a wooden No. 2 and sharpen it with a pocketknife over a metal wastebasket like your grandfather did during the Eisenhower administration.
- Read the full source, not the summary, starting with Man’s Search for Meaning so you can see for yourself which quotes are actually inside it.
- When reviewing a hefty contract, instead of prompting Claude to act “as if you’re my lawyer,” try the radical, ancient analog workflow of hiring an actual lawyer.
- Write your first draft by hand. Write your second draft in wet sand at low tide so you learn non-attachment.
- Set a 10-minute rule: struggle with a problem for 10 minutes before reaching for AI. Then set a 20-minute rule: struggle with the urge to cite Daniel Kahneman before opening X.
- Say it out loud: explain your latest productivity realization to a bartender who cannot legally walk away from his register until you close your tab, and watch his eyes to gauge whether it’s actually profound.
- Memorize a paper highway map and refuse GPS even when you are 18 minutes late to dinner and your wife is staring silently out the passenger window. That icy silence in the front seat? That’s System 2 rebuilding itself in real time.
- Do your own long division on the back of a cocktail napkin at lunch so the table knows you still have skin in the cognitive game.
- Before hitting Post on any essay longer than 500 words, carve it into a slab of limestone with a chisel to test whether humanity truly needed it.
- Replace “grok” with “understand,” replace “&” with “and,” and replace “clean dopamine” with “I felt good about getting my work done.”
- Stare out a window for 15 unbroken minutes with zero inputs, zero podcasts, and zero mental models until you remember that “controlling the space between stimulus and response” used to just be called sitting quietly.
- Never summarize anything again. If a friend asks how a movie was, stand up and recite the entire screenplay from memory with full blocking and lighting cues.
- Treat AI as an “editor,” not a “writer.” That way, when it rewrites every single sentence for you anyway, you can still sleep soundly under the warm blanket of semantics.
- Ask yourself one final question before publishing anything about the future of human cognition: Would Socrates have typed this, or would he have asked for the hemlock twenty minutes early?

AI is like the sun.

Actually, if we’re applying a little System 2 rigor here, AI is nothing like the sun. The sun is a G-type main-sequence star holding eight planets in orbit through gravity that will eventually swell into a red giant and vaporize the earth. AI is a very fast autocomplete machine wired into a warehouse of GPUs that helps people turn a three-sentence email into a keynote about human destiny.

Yes, it may help cure cancer.
Yes, it may put a tutor in every child’s hands.
Yes, it may usher in an age of abundance, starting, apparently, with an unlimited abundance of 900-word essays by executives who just discovered paper and graphite.

It is powerful beyond measure. Which is why we must protect the final frontier of being human at all costs: knowing when to read the contract, put the pencil down, close the laptop, and not write a single word about it on the internet.

Anyway, I’ll be completely honest with you: I didn’t write a single word of this.

I pasted your post into my AI and told it to draft an extremely lengthy quote tweet at least twice as long as yours, because I had better things to do tonight and frankly it seemed funnier than thinking.

We must fight against the death of thought.
title_zh:
他是对的。 我们正在经历思想的死亡。

刚才，我不得不阅读一篇由 AI 生成的 900 字的厚篇文章，内容是关于一个使用自动铅笔打印合同的人。

我没有浏览 12 秒，低声说“对他有好处”，然后继续我的夜晚，而是做了一些激进的事情。

我
full_text_en:
He's right.  We are experiencing the death of thought.

Just now, I had to read a hefty AI-generated 900-word post about a guy who printed a contract and used a mechanical pencil.

Rather than skim it for 12 seconds, whisper “good for him,” and move on with my evening, I did something radical.

I didn’t print your post on a Wi-Fi laser printer like some kind of Silicon Valley soft-hands.

I transcribed every single one of your 902 words by hand onto unbleached calfskin vellum using a goose quill I cured in my own garage, sharpened it with a dull pocketknife until my thumb bled, and spent four and a half hours marking up the margins in homemade iron-gall ink.

I finished writing down my thoughts in the margins, set down my quill, stared silently at a brass lamp, and reflected on what just happened.

I felt deeply satisfied, wildly embarrassed, mildly dehydrated, and somehow taller all at once.

I couldn’t remember the last time I had used my brain for an end-to-end process without relying on an industrial convenience like a mechanical pencil or Hewlett-Packard toner. I felt total command over your post. I felt crystalline clarity about what I understood, what I didn’t understand, and why a grown man felt moved to alert the entire timeline that he had read a PDF with a pencil. And I was left with unshakable conviction in my POV.

Moreover, I felt the high of “ultra-clean” dopamine.

Not the factory-farmed, seed-oil dopamine you get from pressing a plastic thumb-clicker on a 0.7mm Pentel like a lab rat tapping a lever for pellets. Not the lukewarm, ultra-processed dopamine of reading a contract printed out on bleached 20-pound copy paper that a machine collated for you without even asking you to set the movable type.

No. I’m talking about single-origin, cold-pressed, pasture-raised dopamine. The kind of raw, unadulterated neurochemical high our ancestors felt when they sat down at a mahogany desk, read an actual contract from page one to the signature block, and didn’t immediately open LinkedIn to announce that they had survived the ordeal.

Then I felt embarrassed.

How long had I been depriving myself of turning basic adult errands into sweeping civilizational manifestos?

Just yesterday, I made two slices of sourdough toast without once asking Claude to “review this loaf, break down the crumb structure, and give me feedback as if you’re my baker.” I stood there in front of the toaster like a pioneer on the Oregon Trail, watched the heating coils glow orange, buttered the bread manually, and ate it. And what did I do afterward? Nothing. I just rinsed my plate and went to work. Not a single 1,000-word reflection on the erosion of culinary agency. Not one mention of Socrates. Not one bulleted list of ways to reclaim the sacred space between bread and butter.

I was disgusted with myself.

And then I got curious.

In fact, I got so curious that I had to sit down, because curiosity at this altitude can make a man lightheaded.

Why is it that every time somebody in tech rediscovers an office supply from 1987, he feels spiritually compelled to summon Daniel Kahneman, Socrates, and Viktor Frankl like the Avengers? And what can we do to make sure we don’t surrender our last remaining shred of self-awareness to the Thought Leadership Industrial Complex?

The answer lies in what Daniel Kahneman called System 1 and System 2 thinking, and more importantly, in the three higher systems that Kahneman was too polite to put in the book.

Everyone on the internet loves citing System 1 and System 2, mostly because Thinking, Fast and Slow is the single most-referenced book among people who read a four-page summary of it in 2016 and have been dining out on the phrase “lazy controller” ever since.

System 1 is fast, automatic, and gut-driven thought. It’s what fires when a 42-page commercial agreement lands in your inbox on a Thursday afternoon and your brain immediately says, “I am not reading all of this, I should probably pay an actual lawyer instead of asking a chatbot to roleplay as one.”

System 2 is deliberate, analytical, effortful, and conscious. It’s what fires when you ignore System 1, print the 42-page agreement yourself, grab a mechanical pencil, write “check indemnity??” and “what does mutatis mutandis mean” in the margins for 90 minutes, and walk away from your desk feeling like John Marshall presiding over Marbury v. Madison.

But stopping at System 2 is rookie-level cognition. If you really want to diagnose what is happening to the human mind in 2026, you have to go deeper:

System 3 is performing System 2 in public so strangers know you still have a prefrontal cortex. You didn’t merely read the contract. You observed yourself reading the contract from a cinematic third-person camera angle, felt a single noble tear roll down your cheek, and started mentally workshopping the opening hook somewhere around Section 7.2(b).

System 4 is taking a completely normal Tuesday afternoon task (reading a document before you sign it) and laundering it through one ancient Greek philosopher, three cognitive psychologists, a misattributed quote, ten repetitive bullet points, and a closing comparison to the sun until a routine administrative chore sounds like the drafting of the Magna Carta.

System 5 is reading someone else’s System 4 post and concluding that the only proportionate moral response is to construct an even longer, even more grandiose System 4 post, thereby testing the structural load limits of the X Premium character counter and everybody’s patience simultaneously.

Technology has been hijacking effortful thinking for far longer than 370 BC. Frankly, starting the timeline with Socrates is System 1 history.

Roughly a million years ago: Fire hijacked raw-meat mastication as a gastrointestinal System 2 exercise. Early hominids no longer had to chew elk cartilage for four uninterrupted hours just to extract 300 calories. Immediate metabolic offloading. Everything went downhill from there.

3200 BC: Sumerian cuneiform hijacked remembering how many goats your brother-in-law owed you from the spring harvest. Within two generations, nobody could keep track of a single goat in their head. Pure cognitive atrophy.

1440 AD: Gutenberg’s printing press hijacked the deeply satisfying, hard-fought labor of being a medieval monk squinting in an unheated stone scriptorium for eleven years to hand-copy one manuscript by tallow candle. Did anyone pause to ask what the printing press was doing to the monks’ taste?

1784: Bifocals hijacked squinting as an ocular System 2 exercise.

1822: John Isaac Hawkins and Sampson Mordan secured British Patent No. 4742 for the first mechanical pencil, explicitly designed in the words of the patent itself for “rendering the frequent cutting or mending of the points or nibs unnecessary.”

Stop and sit with that for a moment.

The very mechanical pencil you held aloft yesterday as your Excalibur against Silicon Valley is itself a 204-year-old machine engineered to offload the noble, character-building friction of whittling cedarwood with a blade and blowing graphite dust off your thumb. You didn’t reject shortcuts. You just picked a Victorian shortcut and called it enlightenment.

1959: The Xerox 914 photocopier hijacked retyping contracts on carbon paper.

1983: Microsoft Word hijacked Wite-Out and the healthy, adrenaline-soaked terror of making a typo on page 14 of a 15-page lease.

Calculators hijacked long division.
GPS hijacked arguing with your spouse over a folded Rand McNally road atlas on the center console while missing the exit for Savannah.
Google hijacked sitting at a bar for three hours insisting to your friends that Kevin Costner was in Air Force One when it was actually Harrison Ford, the kind of hard-fought, unadulterated barstool conviction that used to build real character.

Now, to be completely fair to you, you’re right about one big thing. AI really is different.

It doesn’t just take over one effortful job at a time. It takes over all of them at once.

Remembering. Summarizing. Researching. Calculating. Writing. Problem-solving. Weighing trade-offs. Deciding. Planning. Navigating people. Reflecting. Creating. Sounding like a 2019 Medium post. Putting “&” instead of “and” ten times inside a 5,300-character essay where nobody was running out of space. Using the verb “grok” unironically in a manifesto about resisting the machines. Building a ten-item bulleted list where four of the bullets are literally the same bullet wearing different sweaters.

For 200,000 years, our brains have been wired to take the easy out. And when we surrender to shortcuts, whether it’s letting an LLM read our contracts or letting LinkedIn formatting do the heavy lifting of sounding profound, we pay a steep price.

Let’s break down the real costs.

Cost 1: A summary feels like understanding, and a numbered framework feels like wisdom.

You’re completely right that reading a compressed summary tricks your brain into believing you understand a subject you never actually wrestled with. What gets overlooked is the mirror-image trap: taking a twelve-word piece of common sense (“If you don’t read the contract, you won’t know what’s in it”) and inflating it into a 900-word lecture about Paleolithic brain evolution tricks both the author and the reader into thinking they just witnessed a breakthrough in epistemology. Packaging isn’t insight. Single-line paragraphs aren’t depth.

Like this.

And this.

Notice how your brain wants to nod slowly right now, even though I haven’t said anything since the previous paragraph. That’s System 1 getting played by line breaks.

Cost 2: The messy middle is the space for growth, which is also where you discover that reviewing a hefty contract without a lawyer is an exciting way to buy a lawsuit.

Robert Bjork’s work on “desirable difficulties” at UCLA is genuinely great research, and Risko and Gilbert’s work on cognitive offloading is real too. Effortful retrieval makes learning stick. Nobody serious disagrees with that. The funny part is acting like desirable difficulty is an endangered species we have to artificially manufacture with “no-AI blocks,” as if real life isn’t already handing out nine hours of involuntary desirable difficulty every single weekday. Try closing a deal with a stubborn lender, managing a payroll when receivables slip, or reading Section 14.3(c) of a commercial lease where the other side quietly buried a personal guaranty inside a boilerplate maintenance clause. You don’t need a 10-minute productivity hack to experience cognitive friction. Just have actual skin in the game.

Cost 3: The disappearance of judgement, and the rise of the performative sigh.

You asked what will stay uniquely human as we approach AGI and ASI, and you gave us four pillars:

1. Intent
2. Accountability
3. Relationships
4. Judgement

Solid start. Respectable list. A little short, though. If we’re being honest about the final frontier of human uniqueness in the age of superintelligence, there are at least six more traits no neural network will ever truly replicate:

5. Printing a 30-page PDF so you can carry it around the house looking burdened and important.
6. Telling everybody at dinner that you’ve “been going really analog lately.”
7. Buying a $65 brass mechanical pencil from a specialty stationery shop in Kyoto so your margin notes have better mouthfeel.
8. Calling regular job satisfaction “clean dopamine” because saying “I felt good about finishing my work” doesn’t sound like a Huberman episode.
9. Assuming that because you used to outsource your thinking to Claude, the rest of Western civilization forgot how to read a document.
10. Confusing “having taste” with “posting about how important taste is.”

Taste really is thousands of compressed System 2 patterns firing at once. You know what one of those patterns looks like? Reading your own draft back before hitting Post and thinking, “Wait, did I really just compare myself reading a contract with a pencil to fighting for the survival of human thought?”

Cost 4: The Viktor Frankl Industrial Complex.

Every serious productivity essay on the internet must, by federal statute, include the exact quote:

“Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom.”

It’s a lovely sentiment. There is just one tiny, delicious wrinkle.

Viktor Frankl never wrote it.

Researchers have searched Man’s Search for Meaning and the rest of Frankl’s published works top to bottom. Those words aren’t there. Stephen Covey popularized the line after coming across a similar passage in a university library book in Hawaii (scholars point to psychologist Rollo May’s 1963 writing on pausing between stimulus and response as the closest precursor), and somewhere around the mid-2000s the internet glued Viktor Frankl’s name onto it and never looked back.

Think about the sheer poetry of that. A few lines above your own bullet point commanding humanity to “Read the full source, not the summary,” you dropped the single most famous misattributed summary-culture quote on the entire internet.

If that isn’t a case study in cognitive offloading, nothing is.

Cost 5: The hyperinflation of metaphors.

Once upon a time, a contract was a contract and the sun was a 4.6-billion-year-old ball of fusing hydrogen plasma 93 million miles from Earth that grows crops, powers the water cycle, and gives you a leathery neck if you skip sunscreen on the back nine.

Now a probabilistic text engine that tells you “That’s a really sharp, nuanced point!” every time you misspell a question is “like the sun.”

If AI is the sun, what does that make the mechanical pencil? A patio umbrella? SPF 50? A pair of polarized sunglasses? Once you start comparing software subscriptions to nuclear fusion in space, you leave yourself nowhere to go when something actually important happens.

Cost 6: The collapse of proportionality.

When every minor personal realization (today I read a document carefully instead of skimming an AI bullet list!) has to be framed as an existential battle at the edge of the species, our collective sense of scale breaks down. Sometimes you didn’t strike a blow against the death of thought. Sometimes you just did your homework.

So how do we take back our thinking, our brevity, and our dignity, while still embracing this transformative technology?

It resolves down to one key principle: rebuild the space between having a normal afternoon and writing a 900-word sermon about it.

How you rebuild that space is completely up to you. Pick your poison:

- Create 30-to-60-minute no-AI blocks in your day, followed immediately by 90-minute no-posting blocks so you don’t undo the entire spiritual benefit by bragging about it online.
- Go analog and print out what matters. Then print out something that doesn’t matter at all, just to maintain dominance over your printer.
- Ditch the mechanical pencil. Use a wooden No. 2 and sharpen it with a pocketknife over a metal wastebasket like your grandfather did during the Eisenhower administration.
- Read the full source, not the summary, starting with Man’s Search for Meaning so you can see for yourself which quotes are actually inside it.
- When reviewing a hefty contract, instead of prompting Claude to act “as if you’re my lawyer,” try the radical, ancient analog workflow of hiring an actual lawyer.
- Write your first draft by hand. Write your second draft in wet sand at low tide so you learn non-attachment.
- Set a 10-minute rule: struggle with a problem for 10 minutes before reaching for AI. Then set a 20-minute rule: struggle with the urge to cite Daniel Kahneman before opening X.
- Say it out loud: explain your latest productivity realization to a bartender who cannot legally walk away from his register until you close your tab, and watch his eyes to gauge whether it’s actually profound.
- Memorize a paper highway map and refuse GPS even when you are 18 minutes late to dinner and your wife is staring silently out the passenger window. That icy silence in the front seat? That’s System 2 rebuilding itself in real time.
- Do your own long division on the back of a cocktail napkin at lunch so the table knows you still have skin in the cognitive game.
- Before hitting Post on any essay longer than 500 words, carve it into a slab of limestone with a chisel to test whether humanity truly needed it.
- Replace “grok” with “understand,” replace “&” with “and,” and replace “clean dopamine” with “I felt good about getting my work done.”
- Stare out a window for 15 unbroken minutes with zero inputs, zero podcasts, and zero mental models until you remember that “controlling the space between stimulus and response” used to just be called sitting quietly.
- Never summarize anything again. If a friend asks how a movie was, stand up and recite the entire screenplay from memory with full blocking and lighting cues.
- Treat AI as an “editor,” not a “writer.” That way, when it rewrites every single sentence for you anyway, you can still sleep soundly under the warm blanket of semantics.
- Ask yourself one final question before publishing anything about the future of human cognition: Would Socrates have typed this, or would he have asked for the hemlock twenty minutes early?

AI is like the sun.

Actually, if we’re applying a little System 2 rigor here, AI is nothing like the sun. The sun is a G-type main-sequence star holding eight planets in orbit through gravity that will eventually swell into a red giant and vaporize the earth. AI is a very fast autocomplete machine wired into a warehouse of GPUs that helps people turn a three-sentence email into a keynote about human destiny.

Yes, it may help cure cancer.
Yes, it may put a tutor in every child’s hands.
Yes, it may usher in an age of abundance, starting, apparently, with an unlimited abundance of 900-word essays by executives who just discovered paper and graphite.

It is powerful beyond measure. Which is why we must protect the final frontier of being human at all costs: knowing when to read the contract, put the pencil down, close the laptop, and not write a single word about it on the internet.

Anyway, I’ll be completely honest with you: I didn’t write a single word of this.

I pasted your post into my AI and told it to draft an extremely lengthy quote tweet at least twice as long as yours, because I had better things to do tonight and frankly it seemed funnier than thinking.

We must fight against the death of thought.
full_text_zh:
他是对的。 我们正在经历思想的死亡。

刚才，我不得不阅读一篇由 AI 生成的 900 字的厚篇文章，内容是关于一个使用自动铅笔打印合同的人。

我没有浏览 12 秒，低声说“对他有好处”，然后继续我的夜晚，而是做了一些激进的事情。

我没有像硅谷的软手那样使用 Wi-Fi 激光打印机打印你的文章。

我用在自家车库里腌制的鹅毛笔，将你的 902 个单词中的每一个字都手写在未漂白的小牛皮牛皮纸上，用钝的小刀将其削尖，直到我的拇指流血，并花了四个半小时用自制的铁胆墨水标记边缘。

我在页边写完自己的想法，放下羽毛笔，默默地盯着一盏铜灯，思考着刚刚发生的事情。

我感到深深的满足、极度的尴尬、轻微的脱水，但不知何故突然长高了。

我不记得上次我在不依赖自动铅笔或惠普碳粉等工业便利设施的情况下使用大脑进行端到端流程是什么时候了。我对你的帖子感到完全掌控。我对自己理解的内容、不理解的内容感到非常清晰，也明白了为什么一个成年人会因为提醒整个时间线他用铅笔阅读了一份 PDF 而感到感动。我对自己的观点有着不可动摇的信念。

此外，我还感受到了“超洁净”多巴胺的快感。

不是工厂化养殖的种子油多巴胺，是通过在 0.7 毫米 Pentel 上按下塑料拇指点击器而获得的，就像实验室老鼠敲击颗粒杠杆一样。阅读打印在漂白的 20 磅复印纸上的合同时，机器会帮你校对，甚至不需要你设置活字印刷，这不是那种不冷不热、经过过度处理的多巴胺。

不，我说的是单一来源、冷榨、牧场饲养的多巴胺。当我们的祖先坐在桃花心木办公桌前，从第一页读到签名栏，阅读一份真实的合同，并且没有立即打开 LinkedIn 宣布他们已经从这场磨难中幸存下来时，他们感受到了那种原始的、纯粹的神经化学物质的兴奋。

然后我就觉得很尴尬。

我已经多久没有把基本的成人事务变成全面的文明宣言了？

就在昨天，我做了两片酵母吐司，一次都没有要求克劳德“检查这条面包，分解面包屑结构，并给我反馈，就像你是我的面包师一样。”我像俄勒冈小道上的拓荒者一样站在烤面包机前，看着加热线圈发出橙色的光，手动在面包上涂黄油，然后吃掉它。然后我做了什么？没有什么。我刚洗完盘子就去上班了。没有一篇关于烹饪机构受到侵蚀的千字反思。没有提到苏格拉底。没有一份详细的清单列出了重新夺回面包和黄油之间神圣空间的方法。

我对自己感到厌恶。

然后我很好奇。

事实上，我实在是太好奇了，不得不坐下来，因为在这种高度的好奇心会让人头晕目眩。

为什么每次科技领域的人重新发现 1987 年的办公用品时，他都会在精神上感到有必要像复仇者联盟一样召唤丹尼尔·卡尼曼、苏格拉底和维克托·弗兰克尔？我们能做些什么来确保我们不会将最后的一点自我意识拱手让给思想领导工业综合体？

答案就在于丹尼尔·卡尼曼所说的“系统1”和“系统2”的思维，更重要的是，在于卡尼曼出于礼貌而没有将其放入书中的三个更高的系统。

互联网上的每个人都喜欢引用系统 1 和系统 2，主要是因为《思考，快与慢》是人们在 2016 年读过该书长达四页的摘要并从那时起就一直在谈论“懒惰控制器”这个词的人中引用最多的一本书。

系统 1 是快速、自动、直觉驱动的思维。当周四下午一份 42 页的商业协议到达你的收件箱时，你的大脑立即说：“我不会阅读所有这些内容，我可能应该付钱给一名真正的律师，而不是让聊天机器人扮演律师。”

系统2是深思熟虑的、分析性的、努力的、有意识的。当你忽略系统 1，自己打印 42 页的协议，拿起自动铅笔，写下“检查赔偿？”时，就会触发这种情况。并在页边空白处写上“比照意味着什么”90 分钟，然后离开办公桌，感觉就像约翰·马歇尔在主持马伯里诉麦迪逊案。

但止步于系统2是菜鸟级别的认知。如果你真的想诊断 2026 年人类思维会发生什么，你必须更深入：

系统 3 在公共场合执行系统 ​​2，因此陌生人知道您仍然有前额皮质。您不仅仅阅读了合同。你观察到自己从电影般的第三人称视角阅读合同，感觉到一滴高贵的泪水从你的脸颊滚落，并开始在脑海中思考第 7.2(b) 节周围的开头钩子。

系统 4 正在执行一项完全正常的周二下午任务（在签署之前阅读一份文件），并通过一位古希腊哲学家、三位认知心理学家、一段错误引用、十个重复的要点以及与太阳的最终比较来对其进行清洗，直到日常行政琐事听起来像是起草《大宪章》。

系统 5 正在阅读其他人的系统 4 帖子，并得出结论，唯一相称的道德反应是构建一个更长、更宏伟的系统 4 帖子，从而同时测试 X Premium 角色计数器的结构负载限制和每个人的耐心。

自公元前 370 年以来，技术一直在劫持努力的思维。坦率地说，从苏格拉底开始的时间线就是系统 1 的历史。

大约一百万年前：火劫持了生肉咀嚼作为胃肠道系统 2 的锻炼。早期原始人类不再需要连续四个小时不间断地咀嚼麋鹿软骨来获取 300 卡路里的热量。立即代谢卸载。从那里开始一切都走下坡路。

公元前 3200 年：苏美尔楔形文字劫持了你的姐夫欠你多少春收的山羊。在两代人的时间里，没有人能够在头脑中记住一只山羊。纯粹的认知萎缩。

公元 1440 年：古腾堡的印刷机劫持了一位中世纪僧侣在没有暖气的石质写字间眯着眼睛用牛油蜡烛手抄一份手稿长达 11 年的令人深感满足的艰苦劳动。有没有人停下来问一下印刷机对僧侣们的口味做了什么？

1784 年：双焦点眼镜劫持了眯眼作为一种视觉系统 2 的锻炼方式。

1822 年：约翰·艾萨克·霍金斯 (John Isaac Hawkins) 和桑普森·莫丹 (Sampson Mordan) 为第一支自动铅笔获得了第 4742 号英国专利，专利本身的明确设计目的是“无需频繁切割或修补笔尖或笔尖”。

停下来坐一会儿。

昨天你在与硅谷对抗时高举的 Excalibur 机械铅笔本身就是一台拥有 204 年历史的机器，其设计目的是为了减轻用刀片削雪松木和吹掉拇指上的石墨粉尘时产生的高贵、塑造性格的摩擦。你没有拒绝捷径。你刚刚选择了一条维多利亚时代的捷径，并称之为启蒙。

1959 年：施乐 914 复印机劫持了在复写纸上重新打印合同的行为。

1983 年：Microsoft Word 劫持了 Wite-Out，以及在 15 页租约的第 14 页上犯错的健康、令人肾上腺素飙升的恐惧。

计算器劫持了长除法。
GPS 被劫持，您与配偶就中控台上折叠的兰德·麦克纳利道路地图集争论，同时错过了萨凡纳的出口。
谷歌劫持了在酒吧坐了三个小时，向你的朋友坚称凯文·科斯特纳在空军一号，而实际上是哈里森·福特，这种经过艰苦斗争、纯粹的酒吧凳信念用来塑造真实的性格。

现在，公平地说，你对一件大事的看法是正确的。人工智能确实不同。

它不仅仅一次接管一项艰苦的工作。它立刻接管了所有的人。

记住。总结一下。研究中。计算。写作。解决问题。权衡利弊。决定。规划。为人们导航。反思。创造。听起来像是 2019 年的 Medium 帖子。在一篇 5,300 字的文章中十次用“&”代替“and”，没有人会出现空间不足的情况。在关于抵抗机器的宣言中讽刺地使用了动词“grok”。建立一个包含十项项目符号的列表，其中四个项目符号实际上是相同的项目符号，穿着不同的毛衣。

20万年来，我们的大脑一直习惯于轻松出行。当我们屈服于捷径时，无论是让法学硕士阅读我们的合同，还是让LinkedIn格式完成听起来深刻的繁重工作，我们都会付出高昂的代价。

让我们来分解一下实际成本。

成本1：总结感觉像是理解，编号框架感觉像是智慧。

你完全正确，阅读压缩摘要会欺骗你的大脑，让你相信你理解了一个你从未真正思考过的主题。被忽视的是镜像陷阱：将一段 12 个字的常识（“如果你不读合同，你不会知道里面有什么”）并将其夸大为关于旧石器时代大脑进化的 900 字讲座，欺骗作者和读者，让他们认为他们刚刚见证了认识论的突破。包装不是洞察力。单行段落没有深度。

像这样。

还有这个。

注意你的大脑现在想要慢慢点头，尽管自上一段以来我没有说过任何话。这就是系统 1 的换行符。

成本2：混乱的中间是成长的空间，这也是你发现在没有律师的情况下审查一份巨额合同是一种令人兴奋的购买诉讼的方式的地方。

罗伯特·比约克（Robert Bjork）在加州大学洛杉矶分校关于“理想困难”的研究确实是伟大的研究，里斯科和吉尔伯特关于认知卸载的研究也是真实的。努力的检索可以使学习坚持下去。没有人认真地反对这一点。有趣的是，我们表现得好像理想难度是一种濒临灭绝的物种，我们必须用“无人工智能块”人为制造，就好像现实生活还没有每个工作日提供九个小时非自愿的理想难度一样。尝试与顽固的贷方达成交易，在应收账款滑落时管理工资，或者阅读商业租赁第 14.3(c) 条，其中另一方悄悄地将个人担保埋在样板维护条款中。你不需要花 10 分钟提高效率来体验认知摩擦。只需在游戏中拥有真实的皮肤即可。

成本3：判断力的消失，表演性叹息的兴起。

您问当我们接近 AGI 和 ASI 时，什么才能保持人类的独特性，您给了我们四个支柱：

1. 意图
2. 问责制
3. 关系
4、判断

扎实的开始。令人尊敬的名单。不过有点短。如果我们诚实地对待超级智能时代人类独特性的最终前沿，那么至少还有六个特征是神经网络无法真正复制的：

5. 打印一份 30 页的 PDF，这样你就可以带着它在家里到处走，看起来既沉重又重要。
6. 在晚餐时告诉大家你“最近一直在进行模拟”。
7. 从京都的一家文具专卖店购买一支 65 美元的黄铜自动铅笔，这样你的页边笔记会有更好的口感。
8. 将正常的工作满意度称为“干净的多巴胺”，因为说“我对完成工作感觉很好”听起来不像休伯曼的插曲。
9. 假设因为你过去把你的思维外包给克劳德，所以西方文明的其他部分忘记了如何阅读文档。
10. 将“有品味”与“发布品味的重要性”混为一谈。

味道实际上是数千个压缩的 System 2 模式同时发射。你知道其中一种图案是什么样子的吗？在点击《邮报》之前，先回顾一下自己的草稿，然后思考：“等等，我真的只是将自己用铅笔阅读一份合同与为人类思想的生存而战进行比较吗？”

成本 4：维克多·弗兰克尔工业园区。

根据联邦法规，互联网上每一篇严肃的生产力文章都必须包含准确的引用：

“刺激和反应之间有一个空间。在这个空间里，我们有能力选择我们的反应。我们的反应就是我们的成长和自由。”

这是一种可爱的情感。只有一条细小的、美味的皱纹。

维克多·弗兰克尔从未写过它。

研究人员从头到尾检索了《人类的意义探寻》和弗兰克尔出版的其他作品。这些话不存在。史蒂芬·柯维 (Stephen Covey) 在夏威夷的一本大学图书馆的书中看到类似的段落后，就普及了这句话（学者们指出，心理学家罗洛·梅 (Rollo May) 1963 年撰写的有关刺激与反应之间暂停的文章是最接近的前兆），大约在 2000 年代中期，互联网将维克多·弗兰克尔 (Viktor Frankl) 的名字贴在上面，再也没有回头。

想想这纯粹的诗意。在你自己的要点之上几行命令人类“阅读完整的源代码，而不是摘要”，你在整个互联网上丢下了最著名的错误总结文化引用。

如果这不是一个关于认知卸载的案例研究，那就没什么了。

成本5：隐喻的过度膨胀。

曾几何时，合同就是合同，太阳是一个 46 亿年前的聚变氢等离子体球，距离地球 9300 万英里，它种植农作物，为水循环提供动力，如果你在后九洞不涂防晒霜，它还会给你一个坚韧的脖子。

现在，概率文本引擎会告诉您“这是一个非常尖锐、微妙的观点！”每次你拼写错误的问题都是“like the sun”。

如果人工智能是太阳，那么自动铅笔又是什么呢？遮阳伞？防晒指数 50？一副偏光太阳镜？一旦你开始将软件订阅与太空中的核聚变进行比较，当真正重要的事情发生时，你就会无处可去。

成本6：比例性的崩溃。

当每一个小小的个人认识（今天我仔细阅读一份文件，而不是浏览人工智能项目符号列表！）都必须被视为物种边缘的一场生存之战时，我们的集体尺度感就崩溃了。有时你没有对思想的死亡进行打击。有时你只是做了作业。

那么，我们如何在拥抱这项变革性技术的同时，收回我们的思考、我们的简洁和我们的尊严呢？

它归结为一个关键原则：重建一个正常的下午和为此写一篇 900 字的布道之间的空间。

如何重建该空间完全取决于您。选择你的毒药：

- 在一天中创建 30 到 60 分钟的无 AI 时段，然后立即进行 90 分钟的无发帖时段，这样您就不会因在网上吹嘘而抵消全部精神益处。
- 进行模拟并打印出重要的内容。然后打印一些根本不重要的东西，只是为了保持对打印机的主导地位。
- 扔掉自动铅笔。使用木制 2 号刀，然后用小刀在金属废纸篓上削尖，就像您祖父在艾森豪威尔政府期间所做的那样。
- 阅读完整的源代码，而不是摘要，从《Man's Search for Meaning》开始，这样你就可以亲眼看到其中实际上包含了哪些引言。
- 在审查一份巨额合同时，不要让克劳德表现得“就像你是我的律师一样”，而是尝试采用激进、古老的模拟工作流程，即聘请一名真正的律师。
- 手写你的初稿。退潮时在湿沙上写下你的第二稿，这样你就能学会不执着。
- 设定 10 分钟规则：在使用 AI 之前先解决一个问题 10 分钟。然后设定一个 20 分钟的规则：在打开 X 之前，克制住引用 Daniel Kahneman 的冲动。
- 大声说出来：向调酒师解释你最新的生产力认识，除非你关闭标签，否则他不能合法地离开他的收银台，并观察他的眼睛来判断它是否真的很深刻。
- 记住纸质高速公路地图并拒绝使用 GPS，即使您晚于晚餐 18 分钟并且您的妻子默默地盯着乘客窗外。前排座位上冰冷的沉默？这就是系统 2 的实时重建。
- 午餐时在鸡尾酒餐巾背面做自己的长除法，这样餐桌上的人就知道你仍然参与到认知游戏中。
- 在发表任何超过 500 字的文章之前，先用凿子将其雕刻在一块石灰石上，以测试人类是否真正需要它。
- 将“grok”替换为“理解”，将“&”替换为“and”，并将“干净的多巴胺”替换为“我对完成工作感觉很好”。
- 不间断地盯着窗外 15 分钟，零输入、零播客和零心理模型，直到您记住“控制刺激和反应之间的空间”过去被称为安静地坐着。
- 永远不要再总结任何事情。如果朋友问一部电影怎么样，请站起来并在完整的遮挡和灯光提示下背诵整个剧本。
- 将人工智能视为“编辑”，而不是“作家”。这样，当它为你重写每一个句子时，你仍然可以在温暖的语义毯下安然入睡。
- 在发表有关人类认知未来的任何内容之前，问自己最后一个问题：苏格拉底会打出这个，还是会提前二十分钟索要铁杉？

人工智能就像太阳。

事实上，如果我们在这里应用一点系统 2 的严格性，人工智能与太阳完全不同。太阳是一颗G型主序恒星，通过引力将八颗行星保持在轨道上，最终将膨胀成红巨星并蒸发地球。人工智能是一种非常快速的自动完成机器，连接到 GPU 仓库中，可以帮助人们将三句话电子邮件变成关于人类命运的主题演讲。

是的，它可能有助于治愈癌症。
是的，它可能会让每个孩子都有一位导师。
是的，它可能会迎来一个丰富的时代，显然，从刚刚发现纸和石墨的高管们撰写的无限丰富的 900 字论文开始。

它的力量强大得难以估量。这就是为什么我们必须不惜一切代价保护人类的最后边界：知道何时阅读合同，放下铅笔，关闭笔记本电脑，而不是在互联网上写下任何有关它的字。

不管怎样，我对你说实话：我一个字都没有写。

我将你的帖子粘贴到我的人工智能中，并告诉它起草一条极其冗长的引用推文，长度至少是你的两倍，因为今晚我有更好的事情要做，坦率地说，这似乎比思考更有趣。

我们必须与思想的死亡作斗争。
author: Coastal Country Club
summary_zh:
没有像硅谷的软手那样使用 Wi-Fi 激光打印机打印你的文章。

我用在自家车库里腌制的鹅毛笔，将你的 902 个单词中的每一个字都手写在未漂白的小牛皮牛皮纸上，用钝的小刀将其削尖，直到我的拇指流血，并花了四个半小时用自制的铁胆墨水标记边缘。

我在页边写完自己的想法，放下羽毛笔，默默地盯着一盏铜灯，思考着刚刚发生的事情。

我感到深深的满足、极度的尴尬、轻微的脱水，但不知何故突然长高了。

我不记得上次我在不依赖自动铅笔或惠普碳粉等工业便利设施的情况下使用大脑进行端到端流程是什么时候了。我对你的帖子感到完全掌控。我对自己理解的内容、不理解的内容感到非常清晰，也明白了为什么一个成年人会因为提醒整个时间线他用铅笔阅读了一份 PDF 而感到感动。我对自己的观点有着不可动摇的信念。

此外，我还感受到了“超洁净”多巴胺的快感。

不是工厂化养殖的种子油多巴胺，是通过在 0.7 毫米 Pentel 上按下塑料拇指点击器而获得的，就像实验室老鼠敲击颗粒杠杆一样。阅读打印在漂白的 20 磅复印纸上的合同时，机器会帮你校对，甚至不需要你设置活字印刷，这不是那种不冷不热、经过过度处理的多巴胺。

不，我说的是单一来源、冷榨、牧场饲养的多巴胺。当我们的祖先坐在桃花心木办公桌前，从第一页读到签名栏，阅读一份真实的合同，并且没有立即打开 LinkedIn 宣布他们已经从这场磨难中幸存下来时，他们感受到了那种原始的、纯粹的神经化学物质的兴奋。

然后我就觉得很尴尬。

我已经多久没有把基本的成人事务变成全面的文明宣言了？

就在昨天，我做了两片酵母吐司，一次都没有要求克劳德“检查这条面包，分解面包屑结构，并给我反馈，就像你是我的面包师一样。”我像俄勒冈小道上的拓荒者一样站在烤面包机前，看着加热线圈发出橙色的光，手动在面包上涂黄油，然后吃掉它。然后我做了什么？没有什么。我刚洗完盘子就去上班了。没有一篇关于烹饪机构受到侵蚀的千字反思。没有提到苏格拉底。没有一份详细的清单列出了重新夺回面包和黄油之间神圣空间的方法。

我对自己感到厌恶。

然后我很好奇。

事实上，我实在是太好奇了，不得不坐下来，因为在这种高度的好奇心会让人头晕目眩。

为什么每次科技领域的人重新发现 1987 年的办公用品时，他都会在精神上感到有必要像复仇者联盟一样召唤丹尼尔·卡尼曼、苏格拉底和维克托·弗兰克尔？我们能做些什么来确保我们不会将最后的一点自我意识拱手让给思想领导工业综合体？

答案就在于丹尼尔·卡尼曼所说的“系统1”和“系统2”的思维，更重要的是，在于卡尼曼出于礼貌而没有将其放入书中的三个更高的系统。

互联网上的每个人都喜欢引用系统 1 和系统 2，主要是因为《思考，快与慢》是人们在 2016 年读过该书长达四页的摘要并从那时起就一直在谈论“懒惰控制器”这个词的人中引用最多的一本书。

系统 1 是快速、自动、直觉驱动的思维。当周四下午一份 42 页的商业协议到达你的收件箱时，你的大脑立即说：“我不会阅读所有这些内容，我可能应该付钱给一名真正的律师，而不是让聊天机器人扮演律师。”

系统2是深思熟虑的、分析性的、努力的、有意识的。当你忽略系统 1，自己打印 42 页的协议，拿起自动铅笔，写下“检查赔偿？”时，就会触发这种情况。并在页边空白处写上“比照意味着什么”90 分钟，然后离开办公桌，感觉就像约翰·马歇尔在主持马伯里诉麦迪逊案。

但止步于系统2是菜鸟级别的认知。如果你真的想诊断 2026 年人类思维会发生什么，你必须更深入：

系统 3 在公共场合执行系统 ​​2，因此陌生人知道您仍然有前额皮质。您不仅仅阅读了合同。你观察到自己从电影般的第三人称视角阅读合同，感觉到一滴高贵的泪水从你的脸颊滚落，并开始在脑海中思考第 7.2(b) 节周围的开头钩子。

系统 4 正在执行一项完全正常的周二下午任务（在签署之前阅读一份文件），并通过一位古希腊哲学家、三位认知心理学家、一段错误引用、十个重复的要点以及与太阳的最终比较来对其进行清洗，直到日常行政琐事听起来像是起草《大宪章》。

系统 5 正在阅读其他人的系统 4 帖子，并得出结论，唯一相称的道德反应是构建一个更长、更宏伟的系统 4 帖子，从而同时测试 X Premium 角色计数器的结构负载限制和每个人的耐心。

自公元前 370 年以来，技术一直在劫持努力的思维。坦率地说，从苏格拉底开始的时间线就是系统 1 的历史。

大约一百万年前：火劫持了生肉咀嚼作为胃肠道系统 2 的锻炼。早期原始人类不再需要连续四个小时不间断地咀嚼麋鹿软骨来获取 300 卡路里的热量。立即代谢卸载。从那里开始一切都走下坡路。

公元前 3200 年：苏美尔楔形文字劫持了你的姐夫欠你多少春收的山羊。在两代人的时间里，没有人能够在头脑中记住一只山羊。纯粹的认知萎缩。

公元 1440 年：古腾堡的印刷机劫持了一位中世纪僧侣在没有暖气的石质写字间眯着眼睛用牛油蜡烛手抄一份手稿长达 11 年的令人深感满足的艰苦劳动。有没有人停下来问一下印刷机对僧侣们的口味做了什么？

1784 年：双焦点眼镜劫持了眯眼作为一种视觉系统 2 的锻炼方式。

1822 年：约翰·艾萨克·霍金斯 (John Isaac Hawkins) 和桑普森·莫丹 (Sampson Mordan) 为第一支自动铅笔获得了第 4742 号英国专利，专利本身的明确设计目的是“无需频繁切割或修补笔尖或笔尖”。

停下来坐一会儿。

昨天你在与硅谷对抗时高举的 Excalibur 机械铅笔本身就是一台拥有 204 年历史的机器，其设计目的是为了减轻用刀片削雪松木和吹掉拇指上的石墨粉尘时产生的高贵、塑造性格的摩擦。你没有拒绝捷径。你刚刚选择了一条维多利亚时代的捷径，并称之为启蒙。

1959 年：施乐 914 复印机劫持了在复写纸上重新打印合同的行为。

1983 年：Microsoft Word 劫持了 Wite-Out，以及在 15 页租约的第 14 页上犯错的健康、令人肾上腺素飙升的恐惧。

计算器劫持了长除法。
GPS 被劫持，您与配偶就中控台上折叠的兰德·麦克纳利道路地图集争论，同时错过了萨凡纳的出口。
谷歌劫持了在酒吧坐了三个小时，向你的朋友坚称凯文·科斯特纳在空军一号，而实际上是哈里森·福特，这种经过艰苦斗争、纯粹的酒吧凳信念用来塑造真实的性格。

现在，公平地说，你对一件大事的看法是正确的。人工智能确实不同。

它不仅仅一次接管一项艰苦的工作。它立刻接管了所有的人。

记住。总结一下。研究中。计算。写作。解决问题。权衡利弊。决定。规划。为人们导航。反思。创造。听起来像是 2019 年的 Medium 帖子。在一篇 5,300 字的文章中十次用“&”代替“and”，没有人会出现空间不足的情况。在关于抵抗机器的宣言中讽刺地使用了动词“grok”。建立一个包含十项项目符号的列表，其中四个项目符号实际上是相同的项目符号，穿着不同的毛衣。

20万年来，我们的大脑一直习惯于轻松出行。当我们屈服于捷径时，无论是让法学硕士阅读我们的合同，还是让LinkedIn格式完成听起来深刻的繁重工作，我们都会付出高昂的代价。

让我们来分解一下实际成本。

成本1：总结感觉像是理解，编号框架感觉像是智慧。

你完全正确，阅读压缩摘要会欺骗你的大脑，让你相信你理解了一个你从未真正思考过的主题。被忽视的是镜像陷阱：将一段 12 个字的常识（“如果你不读合同，你不会知道里面有什么”）并将其夸大为关于旧石器时代大脑进化的 900 字讲座，欺骗作者和读者，让他们认为他们刚刚见证了认识论的突破。包装不是洞察力。单行段落没有深度。

像这样。

还有这个。

注意你的大脑现在想要慢慢点头，尽管自上一段以来我没有说过任何话。这就是系统 1 的换行符。

成本2：混乱的中间是成长的空间，这也是你发现在没有律师的情况下审查一份巨额合同是一种令人兴奋的购买诉讼的方式的地方。

罗伯特·比约克（Robert Bjork）在加州大学洛杉矶分校关于“理想困难”的研究确实是伟大的研究，里斯科和吉尔伯特关于认知卸载的研究也是真实的。努力的检索可以使学习坚持下去。没有人认真地反对这一点。有趣的是，我们表现得好像理想难度是一种濒临灭绝的物种，我们必须用“无人工智能块”人为制造，就好像现实生活还没有每个工作日提供九个小时非自愿的理想难度一样。尝试与顽固的贷方达成交易，在应收账款滑落时管理工资，或者阅读商业租赁第 14.3(c) 条，其中另一方悄悄地将个人担保埋在样板维护条款中。你不需要花 10 分钟提高效率来体验认知摩擦。只需在游戏中拥有真实的皮肤即可。

成本3：判断力的消失，表演性叹息的兴起。

您问当我们接近 AGI 和 ASI 时，什么才能保持人类的独特性，您给了我们四个支柱：

1. 意图
2. 问责制
3. 关系
4、判断

扎实的开始。令人尊敬的名单。不过有点短。如果我们诚实地对待超级智能时代人类独特性的最终前沿，那么至少还有六个特征是神经网络无法真正复制的：

5. 打印一份 30 页的 PDF，这样你就可以带着它在家里到处走，看起来既沉重又重要。
6. 在晚餐时告诉大家你“最近一直在进行模拟”。
7. 从京都的一家文具专卖店购买一支 65 美元的黄铜自动铅笔，这样你的页边笔记会有更好的口感。
8. 将正常的工作满意度称为“干净的多巴胺”，因为说“我对完成工作感觉很好”听起来不像休伯曼的插曲。
9. 假设因为你过去把你的思维外包给克劳德，所以西方文明的其他部分忘记了如何阅读文档。
10. 将“有品味”与“发布品味的重要性”混为一谈。

味道实际上是数千个压缩的 System 2 模式同时发射。你知道其中一种图案是什么样子的吗？在点击《邮报》之前，先回顾一下自己的草稿，然后思考：“等等，我真的只是将自己用铅笔阅读一份合同与为人类思想的生存而战进行比较吗？”

成本 4：维克多·弗兰克尔工业园区。

根据联邦法规，互联网上每一篇严肃的生产力文章都必须包含准确的引用：

“刺激和反应之间有一个空间。在这个空间里，我们有能力选择我们的反应。我们的反应就是我们的成长和自由。”

这是一种可爱的情感。只有一条细小的、美味的皱纹。

维克多·弗兰克尔从未写过它。

研究人员从头到尾检索了《人类的意义探寻》和弗兰克尔出版的其他作品。这些话不存在。史蒂芬·柯维 (Stephen Covey) 在夏威夷的一本大学图书馆的书中看到类似的段落后，就普及了这句话（学者们指出，心理学家罗洛·梅 (Rollo May) 1963 年撰写的有关刺激与反应之间暂停的文章是最接近的前兆），大约在 2000 年代中期，互联网将维克多·弗兰克尔 (Viktor Frankl) 的名字贴在上面，再也没有回头。

想想这纯粹的诗意。在你自己的要点之上几行命令人类“阅读完整的源代码，而不是摘要”，你在整个互联网上丢下了最著名的错误总结文化引用。

如果这不是一个关于认知卸载的案例研究，那就没什么了。

成本5：隐喻的过度膨胀。

曾几何时，合同就是合同，太阳是一个 46 亿年前的聚变氢等离子体球，距离地球 9300 万英里，它种植农作物，为水循环提供动力，如果你在后九洞不涂防晒霜，它还会给你一个坚韧的脖子。

现在，概率文本引擎会告诉您“这是一个非常尖锐、微妙的观点！”每次你拼写错误的问题都是“like the sun”。

如果人工智能是太阳，那么自动铅笔又是什么呢？遮阳伞？防晒指数 50？一副偏光太阳镜？一旦你开始将软件订阅与太空中的核聚变进行比较，当真正重要的事情发生时，你就会无处可去。

成本6：比例性的崩溃。

当每一个小小的个人认识（今天我仔细阅读一份文件，而不是浏览人工智能项目符号列表！）都必须被视为物种边缘的一场生存之战时，我们的集体尺度感就崩溃了。有时你没有对思想的死亡进行打击。有时你只是做了作业。

那么，我们如何在拥抱这项变革性技术的同时，收回我们的思考、我们的简洁和我们的尊严呢？

它归结为一个关键原则：重建一个正常的下午和为此写一篇 900 字的布道之间的空间。

如何重建该空间完全取决于您。选择你的毒药：

- 在一天中创建 30 到 60 分钟的无 AI 时段，然后立即进行 90 分钟的无发帖时段，这样您就不会因在网上吹嘘而抵消全部精神益处。
- 进行模拟并打印出重要的内容。然后打印一些根本不重要的东西，只是为了保持对打印机的主导地位。
- 扔掉自动铅笔。使用木制 2 号刀，然后用小刀在金属废纸篓上削尖，就像您祖父在艾森豪威尔政府期间所做的那样。
- 阅读完整的源代码，而不是摘要，从《Man's Search for Meaning》开始，这样你就可以亲眼看到其中实际上包含了哪些引言。
- 在审查一份巨额合同时，不要让克劳德表现得“就像你是我的律师一样”，而是尝试采用激进、古老的模拟工作流程，即聘请一名真正的律师。
- 手写你的初稿。退潮时在湿沙上写下你的第二稿，这样你就能学会不执着。
- 设定 10 分钟规则：在使用 AI 之前先解决一个问题 10 分钟。然后设定一个 20 分钟的规则：在打开 X 之前，克制住引用 Daniel Kahneman 的冲动。
- 大声说出来：向调酒师解释你最新的生产力认识，除非你关闭标签，否则他不能合法地离开他的收银台，并观察他的眼睛来判断它是否真的很深刻。
- 记住纸质高速公路地图并拒绝使用 GPS，即使您晚于晚餐 18 分钟并且您的妻子默默地盯着乘客窗外。前排座位上冰冷的沉默？这就是系统 2 的实时重建。
- 午餐时在鸡尾酒餐巾背面做自己的长除法，这样餐桌上的人就知道你仍然参与到认知游戏中。
- 在发表任何超过 500 字的文章之前，先用凿子将其雕刻在一块石灰石上，以测试人类是否真正需要它。
- 将“grok”替换为“理解”，将“&”替换为“and”，并将“干净的多巴胺”替换为“我对完成工作感觉很好”。
- 不间断地盯着窗外 15 分钟，零输入、零播客和零心理模型，直到您记住“控制刺激和反应之间的空间”过去被称为安静地坐着。
- 永远不要再总结任何事情。如果朋友问一部电影怎么样，请站起来并在完整的遮挡和灯光提示下背诵整个剧本。
- 将人工智能视为“编辑”，而不是“作家”。这样，当它为你重写每一个句子时，你仍然可以在温暖的语义毯下安然入睡。
- 在发表有关人类认知未来的任何内容之前，问自己最后一个问题：苏格拉底会打出这个，还是会提前二十分钟索要铁杉？

人工智能就像太阳。

事实上，如果我们在这里应用一点系统 2 的严格性，人工智能与太阳完全不同。太阳是一颗G型主序恒星，通过引力将八颗行星保持在轨道上，最终将膨胀成红巨星并蒸发地球。人工智能是一种非常快速的自动完成机器，连接到 GPU 仓库中，可以帮助人们将三句话电子邮件变成关于人类命运的主题演讲。

是的，它可能有助于治愈癌症。
是的，它可能会让每个孩子都有一位导师。
是的，它可能会迎来一个丰富的时代，显然，从刚刚发现纸和石墨的高管们撰写的无限丰富的 900 字论文开始。

它的力量强大得难以估量。这就是为什么我们必须不惜一切代价保护人类的最后边界：知道何时阅读合同，放下铅笔，关闭笔记本电脑，而不是在互联网上写下任何有关它的字。

不管怎样，我对你说实话：我一个字都没有写。

我将你的帖子粘贴到我的人工智能中，并告诉它起草一条极其冗长的引用推文，长度至少是你的两倍，因为今晚我有更好的事情要做，坦率地说，这似乎比思考更有趣。

我们必须与思想的死亡作斗争。

title_en:
@FutureJurvetson @elonmusk @kimmonismus Context:
"I've tried to train models to do video prediction for the better part of the last 20 years, and largely failing for the first 15. Until I realized you had to abandon generative models and use joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPA)" 

"Things started to work in the last few years with JEPA and world models. The main applications are in the physical world, robotics, and industrial process control. Things that Meta is not particularly interested in" 

But my project always had the support of Zuck, Boz, Schrep, and Chris Cox. 

It's true that, as Chief AI Scientist, I was at senior VP level but was an IC. Best job in the company! 

Also true that I never worked on LLMs. I was very supportive of LLM projects at FAIR (e.g. the project that became Llama), and played a role on convincing Mark to create an AI-first product division around Llama, and pushed to open source Llama-2. But I was never involved at the technical level.

title: SBI's ₹1.6 crore offer for a Chief AI Officer is awesome but it also shows how broken PSU bank pay is for tech talent.
title_en:
SBI's ₹1.6 crore offer for a Chief AI Officer is awesome but it also shows how broken PSU bank pay is for tech talent.

Now, SBI is India's biggest bank. Its balance sheet crossed ₹66 lakh crore this year. Almost every Indian family has some link to it, a salary account, a home loan, a pension.

In October, SBI put out an ad for six AI and tech roles. There is one opening for "General Manager and Chief AI Officer".

The pay is up to ₹1.6 crore a year. SBI says it depends on experience, current pay and posting.

The other five roles pay well too. Three Deputy General Managers get up to ₹1.2 crore each. Two AI architects get up to ₹90 lakh each.

Now SBI's own chairman, CS Setty drew ₹63.87 lakh in FY25. So the AI chief can earn about 2.5 times the person who runs the bank.

Yet, private banks are a different world. 

HDFC Bank's CEO Sashidhar Jagdishan was paid ₹12.08 crore in FY25. PSU bank CEOs earn only about 5 to 7% of what private bank CEOs earn.

But SBI able to pay its AI chief more than its chairman, because the role is a contract job. It is a three year term, which SBI can extend by two more years.

Basically, it is the workaround. An AI leader at this level won't come at this budget. So SBI is working around it.

As per the ad, the person will set up control rooms for AI and data products with the business teams. They will track how live AI models perform and what risks they carry. 

They will also run a separate team whose job is to check models independently. They will also train staff to use these tools. The role also covers an enterprise AI platform for generative AI and AI agents.

They need at least 15 years in banking, financial services or IT. And at least 3 years in a senior leadership role in AI, analytics, model oversight or governance.

So a brilliant engineer who built great models alone, but never ran a team, can't apply for this.

Honestly, a three year term is very short for building an AI platform inside a bank this size. SBI should use the two year extension while they build a second line of leaders under the CAIO from day one.

Obviously, a chairman earning less than half of what a new hire under him can earn is not a healthy setup. 

The Finance Ministry should let PSU banks pay market rates for specialist roles through a clear policy, instead of a contract workaround every time.

And if you are a senior data or analytics person who wants a role like this in five years, it rewards people who have led teams, owned model risk and worked with business heads. 

Pure technical depth won't be enough.

full_text_zh:
SBI 为首席人工智能官提供的 1.6 亿卢比的报价很棒，但这也表明 PSU 银行对技术人才的薪酬是多么的破碎。

现在，SBI 是印度最大的银行。今年其资产负债表超过 660 亿卢比。几乎每个印度家庭都与它有某种联系，工资账户、住房贷款、养老金。

10 月，SBI 发布了一则招聘 6 个人工智能和技术职位的广告。有一个“总经理兼首席人工智能官”的职位空缺。

年薪高达 1600 万卢比。 SBI 表示，这取决于经验、当前薪酬和职位。

其他五个角色的报酬也不错。三名副总经理每人的薪酬最高可达 12 万卢比。两名人工智能架构师每人可获得高达 900 万卢比的奖金。

CS Setty 现任 SBI 董事长，2025 财年收入达 638.7 万卢比。因此，人工智能主管的收入大约是银行经营者的 2.5 倍。

然而，私人银行却是一个不同的世界。

HDFC 银行首席执行官 Sashidhar Jagdishan 在 2025 财年的薪酬为 1.208 亿卢比。 PSU 银行首席执行官的收入仅为私人银行首席执行官的 5% 至 7% 左右。

但 SBI 能够向 AI 主管支付比董事长更高的薪酬，因为该职位是合同制工作。任期三年，SBI 可以再延长两年。

基本上，这是解决方法。这个级别的人工智能领导者不会有这样的预算。因此，SBI 正在解决这个问题。

根据广告，此人将与业务团队一起建立人工智能和数据产品的控制室。他们将跟踪实时人工智能模型的表现以及它们带来的风险。

他们还将管理一个单独的团队，其工作是独立检查模型。他们还将培训员工使用这些工具。该角色还涵盖用于生成人工智能和人工智能代理的企业人工智能平台。

他们需要在银行、金融服务或 IT 行业工作至少 15 年。并在人工智能、分析、模型监督或治理领域担任高级领导职务至少 3 年。

因此，一位才华横溢的工程师独自构建了出色的模型，但从未管理过团队，因此无法申请此职位。

老实说，对于在这种规模的银行内部构建人工智能平台来说，三年的期限非常短。 SBI 应该利用两年的延期，从第一天起就在 CAIO 下建立第二线领导人。

显然，董事长的收入还不到他手下新员工收入的一半，这并不是一个健康的设置。

财政部应该通过明确的政策，让事业单位银行为专家角色支付市场利率，而不是每次都通过合同解决办法。

如果你是一名高级数据或分析人员，希望在五年内担任这样的职位，那么它会奖励那些领导团队、承担模型风险并与业务主管合作的人。

纯粹的技术深度是不够的。

如果你是一名高级数据或分析人员，希望在五年内担任这样的职位，那么它会奖励那些领导团队、承担模型风险并与业务主管合作的人。

纯粹的技术深度是不够的。

title_en:
@TheSadMan25 @RajeswarSai I did not make a bet against LLMs.
I supported research on LLMs at FAIR.
Meta made a big bet on LLMs and dialog systems, first as a research project since 2014, then as a product line since 2023 with Llama 2, 3, and 4.
I was never involved in the product effort.
I was not involved in management since 2018, I was an IC, preferring to concentrate on research in SSL and world models.
Llama-4 was a disappointment, largely because time pressure made the team overly conservative. 
My new company is focusing on world models and doing fine, thank you very much.

@TheSadMan25 @RajeswarSai I did not make a bet against LLMs.
I supported research on LLMs at FAIR.
Meta made a big bet on LLMs and dialog systems, first as a research project since 2014, then as a product line since 2023 with Llama 2, 3, and 4.
I was never involved in the product effort.
I was not involved in management since 2018, I was an IC, preferring to concentrate on research in SSL and world models.
Llama-4 was a disappointment, largely because time pressure made the team overly conservative. 
My new company is focusing on world models and doing fine, thank you very much.
full_text_zh:
@TheSadMan25 @RajeswarSai 我没有打赌法学硕士。
我支持 FAIR 的法学硕士研究。
Meta 在法学硕士和对话系统上下了很大的赌注，首先从 2014 年开始作为一个研究项目，然后从 2023 年开始作为 Llama 2、3 和 4 的产品线。
我从未参与过产品工作。
我从2018年开始就没有参与管理，我是一名IC，更喜欢专注于SSL和世界模型的研究。
Llama-4 令人失望，主要是因为时间压力使团队过于保守。
我的新公司专注于世界模特并且做得很好，非常感谢。

title:
TOTALLY  COOKED

Brooke is a perfect case study in what happens when climate alarmism fully liquefies a person’s capacit
title_en:
TOTALLY  COOKED

Brooke is a perfect case study in what happens when climate alarmism fully liquefies a person’s capacity for rational thought. 

She has, quite literally, lost the ability to process basic data and has instead retreated into a cult that requires constant existential dread as proof of membership.

The data is clear  -  the numbers are not ambiguous. 

We have never been safer from climate-related disasters at any point in human history. The chance of dying from one is more than 98% lower than it was a century ago. 

Every major indicator shows the opposite of the apocalypse she has been trained to fear: sustained global greening, declining disaster mortality, and a climate that has been slowly recovering from the Little Ice Age.

We should be rejoicing. 

None of this is secret. It is simply inconvenient to the business model of the climate grifters and the media outlets (ABC and the rest of the usual suspects) that amplify them. 

Brooke has been so thoroughly propagandized that she is now “genuinely afraid for her life” over a risk that has collapsed by an order of magnitude. 

That is not awareness. That is the intellectual equivalent of still believing in monsters under the bed long after the lights have been turned on and the data presented.

By choosing to remain in that state, she is no longer merely harming herself. 

For one can live a full, productive life while they are "genuinely afraid for their lives".

Further, she is harming other impressionable people who might be influenced by her emotional fact-free nonsense and fall into the same self-inflicted neurosis.

The only remaining hope is that some residual capacity for independent thought still exists and that Brooke eventually develops the curiosity—or at least the self-respect—actually read the Evidenve and leave the cult.

full_text_zh:
完全煮熟

布鲁克是一个完美的案例，研究了当气候危言耸听完全削弱一个人的理性思考能力时会发生什么。

毫不夸张地说，她已经失去了处理基本数据的能力，而是退回到一个需要持续存在的恐惧作为其成员身份的证明的邪教中。

数据很清楚——数字并不含糊。

在人类历史上的任何时候，我们从未如此安全地免受与气候相关的灾难的影响。与一个世纪前相比，死于这种疾病的几率降低了 98% 以上。

每一项主要指标都显示出与她所害怕的世界末日相反的一面：全球持续绿化、灾害死亡率下降，以及从小冰河时代缓慢恢复的气候。

我们应该庆幸。

这些都不是秘密。这对于气候欺诈者和放大他们的媒体机构（美国广播公司和其他通常的嫌疑人）的商业模式来说根本不方便。

布鲁克受到了如此彻底的宣传，以至于她现在“真正担心自己的生命安全”，因为风险已经下降了一个数量级。

那不是意识。这相当于在灯打开、数据呈现很久之后仍然相信床底下有怪物。

通过选择保持这种状态，她不再只是在伤害自己。

因为当一个人“真正担心自己的生命安全”时，他们仍然可以过上充实、富有成效的生活。

此外，她正在伤害其他易受影响的人，这些人可能会受到她情感上与事实无关的胡言乱语的影响，并陷入同样的​​自我造成的神经症。

唯一剩下的希望是，一些独立思考的残余能力仍然存在，布鲁克最终会产生好奇心——或者至少是自尊——真正阅读《证据》并离开邪教。

布鲁克受到了如此彻底的宣传，以至于她现在“真正担心自己的生命安全”，因为风险已经下降了一个数量级。

那不是意识。这相当于在灯打开、数据呈现很久之后仍然相信床底下有怪物。

通过选择保持这种状态，她不再只是在伤害自己。

因为当一个人“真正担心自己的生命安全”时，他们仍然可以过上充实、富有成效的生活。

此外，她正在伤害其他易受影响的人，这些人可能会受到她情感上与事实无关的胡言乱语的影响，并陷入同样的​​自我造成的神经症。

唯一剩下的希望是，一些独立思考的残余能力仍然存在，布鲁克最终会产生好奇心——或者至少是自尊——真正阅读《证据》并离开邪教。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 初创公司Thinky Machines发布Inkling 2 Mini模型，该模型总参数量为26.4B，在Agent Arena基准测试中以996分跃居榜单第18位，位列美国开源模型第3名。相比其594B参数量的Small版本，该小型化模型在保持高智能体任务处理能力的同时，显著降低了推理算力门槛。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Thinky Machines launched the Inkling 2 Mini model with 26.4B parameters, ranking 18th on the Agent Arena index and 3rd among U.S. open-weight models. Compared to the 594B parameter Small version, this miniaturized model maintains high performance in agentic tasks while significantly reducing inference compute requirements.

elements_zh.where: Agent Arena评估榜单
elements_zh.what: 发布参数量26.4B的Inkling 2 Mini模型
elements_zh.why: 旨在通过参数剪枝实现高效的智能体任务推理

elements_en.what: Released 26.4B Inkling 2 Mini model
elements_en.why: To achieve efficient agentic reasoning through parameter optimization

ai_analysis.insight_zh: Inkling 2 Mini的成功验证了智能体专用模型（Agentic Models）在参数缩减后仍能保持强劲逻辑表现的技术路径。在当前大模型向端侧部署迁移的趋势下，此类模型通过牺牲非必要参数换取高推理效率，将直接冲击中小型垂直AI应用的市场竞争格局。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The success of Inkling 2 Mini validates the technical trajectory of agent-specific models that maintain strong reasoning despite smaller parameter counts. As LLMs shift towards edge deployment, such models, which exchange redundant parameters for high inference efficiency, will disrupt the market for mid-to-small vertical AI applications.

title: Attackers use AI agent swarms to exploit vulnerabilities in hours. Patches take weeks. Today, Cisco & OpenAI launch Shirudo, an open-source platform that uses eBPF to shield running Linux systems at machine speed without disruptions. Read more: https://t.c
title_en: Attackers use AI agent swarms to exploit vulnerabilities in hours. Patches take weeks. Today, Cisco & OpenAI launch Shirudo, an open-source platform that uses eBPF to shield running Linux systems at machine speed without disruptions. Read more: https://t.c
title_zh: 思科与OpenAI发布开源平台Shirudo
author: @CiscoSecure
summary_en: Cisco and OpenAI have launched Shirudo, an open-source security platform utilizing eBPF technology. The platform is designed to defend against vulnerabilities exploited by AI agent swarms at machine speed, closing the critical protection gap between vulnerability discovery and patch deployment.
summary_zh: 思科与OpenAI联合推出基于eBPF的开源平台Shirudo，旨在抵御AI智能体群发起的系统安全威胁。
full_text_zh: 攻击者使用人工智能代理群在数小时内利用漏洞。补丁需要数周时间。今天，思科和 OpenAI 推出了 Shirudo，这是一个开源平台，它使用 eBPF 来保护以机器速度运行的 Linux 系统而不会造成中断。了解更多：https://t.c

full_text_en: Attackers use AI agent swarms to exploit vulnerabilities in hours. Patches take weeks. Today, Cisco & OpenAI launch Shirudo, an open-source platform that uses eBPF to shield running Linux systems at machine speed without disruptions. Read more: https://t.c
quote_en: Attackers use AI agent swarms to exploit vulnerabilities in hours. Patches take weeks. Today, Cisco & OpenAI launch Shirudo, an open-source platform that uses eBPF to shield running Linux systems at m

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 思科（Cisco）与OpenAI共同发布开源安全平台Shirudo。该平台集成eBPF（扩展伯克利数据包过滤器）技术，旨在解决AI智能体群（Agent Swarms）在短时间内大规模挖掘漏洞并实施攻击的问题，通过在机器层面实现快速拦截补丁部署延迟带来的防御空窗期。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Cisco and OpenAI have launched Shirudo, an open-source security platform utilizing eBPF technology. The platform is designed to defend against vulnerabilities exploited by AI agent swarms at machine speed, closing the critical protection gap between vulnerability discovery and patch deployment.

elements_zh.where: 企业安全防护系统
elements_zh.what: 发布Shirudo开源安全平台
elements_zh.why: 针对AI智能体群攻击的提速，应对现有补丁分发机制的滞后性

elements_en.what: Launched open-source security platform Shirudo
elements_en.why: To counter the rapid exploit capabilities of AI agent swarms and address patch latency

ai_analysis.insight_zh: Shirudo的发布揭示了网络安全防御范式的重大转折，即从人机协同防御转向机机对抗。利用eBPF在内核态实现实时防御，标志着大型科技公司正尝试通过技术架构底层化来对抗AI自动化攻击，未来网络安全行业的护城河将取决于其对内核级防御规则集的掌控能力。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The launch of Shirudo marks a major paradigm shift in cybersecurity from human-in-the-loop to machine-to-machine defense. Utilizing eBPF for real-time protection at the kernel level signals that major tech firms are moving to fight automated AI attacks via low-level architectural control, positioning control over kernel-level defense rules as the new industry moat.

title: GPT-6.2 has an incredible understanding of the 3D world:
title_en: GPT-6.2 has an incredible understanding of the 3D world:
title_zh: OpenAI发布GPT-6.2模型系列，强化三维仿真与工程自动化
author: Greg Brockman
author_role: OpenAI 总裁兼联合创始人
summary_en: OpenAI released the GPT-6.2 model series, featuring the Astra model which achieved a leading 1,318 Elo score on the AA-3D benchmark. By integrating multimodal inputs with external software control, Astra enables end-to-end engineering workflows ranging from sketches to CAD modeling and mechanical simulation.
summary_zh: OpenAI于2026年11月17日推出GPT-6.2系列，包括专业级Astra与轻量级Sol模型，旨在通过多模态感知与工具调用实现三维世界建模与工程自动化。
full_text_zh: GPT-6.2 对 3D 世界有着令人难以置信的理解：
full_text_en: GPT-6.2 has an incredible understanding of the 3D world:

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: OpenAI发布GPT-6.2系列模型，其中Astra模型在AA-3D三维基准测试中以1318 Elo分位列第一。该模型通过集成多模态输入与外部软件控制能力，能够完成从草图到CAD零件设计及Python力学求解的全链路工程任务。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: OpenAI released the GPT-6.2 model series, featuring the Astra model which achieved a leading 1,318 Elo score on the AA-3D benchmark. By integrating multimodal inputs with external software control, Astra enables end-to-end engineering workflows ranging from sketches to CAD modeling and mechanical simulation.

elements_zh.what: 发布GPT-6.2模型系列（Astra与Sol），具备三维场景生成与多步工具链控制能力
elements_zh.why: 降低科学研究与工业设计中的多步仿真成本，优化计算资源分配

ai_analysis.insight_en: OpenAI's tiered strategy with Astra and Sol accelerates the transition of AI from language logic to physical world simulation and automated productivity. ai_analysis.takeaway_zh: OpenAI通过Astra与Sol的差异化分层策略，加速了AI从语言逻辑向物理世界仿真与自动化生产力的跨越。这一技术路线将对传统CAD/CAE软件生态产生降维打击，标志着AI模型正从“信息处理”向“工业制造引擎”演进，重塑汽车、建筑与精密制造的研发效率基准。
ai_analysis.takeaway_en: OpenAI's tiered strategy with Astra and Sol accelerates the transition of AI from language logic to physical world simulation and automated productivity. This trajectory threatens to disrupt legacy CAD/CAE software ecosystems, marking a shift toward AI as an industrial manufacturing engine that redefines R&D benchmarks in automotive and architecture.

title:
Your analytics might be lying to you.

An AI agent can visit your docs, execute commands through your CLI, call your API
title_en:
Your analytics might be lying to you.

An AI agent can visit your docs, execute commands through your CLI, call your API, interact with MCP and open your product in a browser.

Your analytics sees 5 unrelated visitors.

Agentrail just published research showing how to reconstruct these journeys across different surfaces.

12,000 production agent runs tested:

→ 0.750 B³ F1 vs 0.409 with traditional 30-min sessions
→ 0 errors across 2,193 judged proof links
We're going to need a completely different way to understand product traffic.

title: A misunderstanding from this post. This is true organic demand. We haven't yet started routing traffic to Neon by defaul
title_en: A misunderstanding from this post. This is true organic demand. We haven't yet started routing traffic to Neon by default. So, this is users voting with their feet. The change is largely coming through users switching from Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.2.
title_zh: 这篇文章的误解。这是真正的有机需求。默认情况下，我们尚未开始将流量路由到 Neon。所以，这就是用户用脚投票。这一变化主要是由于用户从 Opus 5.5 和 Sol 6.2 切换而来。

title:
Do yourself a favor!

Pick one painful, boring workflow in your company and build an agent that fixes it. Then do it pro
title_en:
Do yourself a favor!

Pick one painful, boring workflow in your company and build an agent that fixes it. Then do it properly:

• Write down how your best person does it today
• Write the spec before the agent writes any code
• If you can write the rule down, make it code instead of an LLM call
• Use the team's own wrong answers from last quarter as the test set
• Score the agent on that test set before anyone relies on it
• Run it in your own cloud tenant so the data stays put
• Give it read access first and write access later
• Make a person approve anything that moves money, emails a customer or deletes data
• Cap every run on time and cost
• Log every model call, tool call and decision
• Track cost per finished task
• Run it alongside the people doing the job for a few weeks and compare
• Turn every complaint into a new test case
• Block changes when the test score drops
• Keep the old process alive until the numbers hold
• Tell the team what it's for before it ships
• Give it one month, then decide

Say the workflow is invoice coding and your team caught 40 wrong codes last quarter. Those 40 are your test set. If the agent gets 37 right, the 3 it misses usually show you a rule nobody wrote down. That's worth finding even if you never ship the agent.

Most of what I've learned from 40 AI agents in production fits on this list.

Do the first one end to end, and the second goes a lot faster because the test set, the logging and the approvals already exist.

full_text_zh:
帮自己一个忙！

选择公司中一个痛苦、无聊的工作流程，并构建一个代理来修复它。然后正确地做：

• 写下你最好的人今天是如何做的
• 在代理编写任何代码之前编写规范
• 如果您可以写下规则，请将其编码而不是LLM调用
• 使用团队自己上季度的错误答案作为测试集
• 在任何人依赖该测试集之前对代理进行评分
• 在您自己的云租户中运行它，以便数据保持不变
• 首先授予其读取权限，然后授予写入权限
• 让某人批准任何转移资金、向客户发送电子邮件或删除数据的行为
• 限制每次运行的时间和成本
• 记录每个模型调用、工具调用和决策
• 跟踪每个已完成任务的成本
• 与从事这项工作的人员一起运行几周并进行比较
• 将每一个投诉转化为一个新的测试用例
• 当测试分数下降时阻止更改
• 保持旧进程处于活动状态，直到数字保持不变
• 在发货前告诉团队它的用途
• 给它一个月的时间，然后再决定

假设工作流程是发票编码，您的团队上季度发现了 40 个错误代码。这 40 个是您的测试集。如果智能体答对了 37 个，那么它错过的 3 个通常会向您显示一条没人写下来的规则。即使您从未运送过代理，这也是值得找到的。

我从 40 个生产中的人工智能代理那里学到的大部分知识都符合这个列表。

端到端地执行第一个操作，第二个操作要快得多，因为测试集、日志记录和批准已经存在。

title: OUT NOW - @GavinSBaker on why the market was voting with its feet for Jensen, why investors are missing a BIG part of AI
title_en:
OUT NOW - @GavinSBaker on why the market was voting with its feet for Jensen, why investors are missing a BIG part of AI ROI, and his bull case for semi stocks during a market panic 

Apple https://t.co/lKqt4TEm5X
Spotify https://t.co/s6b6i3HCWY
YouTube https://t.co/MCiJFUJDpL
Sponsor https://t.co/f3dipJ42co

Gavin's point is that there are lots of companies generating lots of revenue with open source models, and that those substantial figures are not counted in the "Anthropic Plus OpenAI Plus Grok/Gemini ARR" calculations many investors use to estimate ROI of AI CapEx. 

He says second derivative of AI CapEx has "probably peaked" and that "the market is very focused on the second derivative..." but he thinks this will be "a semiconductor cycle much longer than what's in recent memory," and that the AI build-out "may end up being more like the railroads," which were a big chunk of American GDP for ~60 years.

Recorded at @TomorrowXSummit, November 18th, after Nvidia earnings and before Jensen's reinstatement today.

ai_analysis.insight_en: By releasing gBench, Google seeks to establish influence over open-source model evaluation standards. title_en:
I just completed Introduction to AI Security at AISEC University, and here are some of the areas I explored:

• AI Security 
• Data poisoning and training data risks.
• Prompt injection and LLM security.
• Adversarial attacks.
• Model extraction, intellectual property, and privacy risks.
• AI supply chain security.
• Securing AI systems in production.
• AI governance, risk, compliance and security.

One thing that stood out to me is that securing AI goes beyond securing the technology.

It also involves protecting the data, understanding the risks, managing third-party dependencies, and putting the right governance and controls in place.

AI adoption is growing, and security needs to grow alongside it and that's one of the reasons I'm exploring this area

Up next, AI Cybersecurity and Governance

#AIGovernance

title_en:
Good night, Familia.

We need to understand this and note what is important.

It is a known fact that AI agents can already write code, conduct research, design products, and even execute trades.

Unfortunately, something is still missing in the sense that how do they hire each other, deliver work, verify results, and receive payments without humans coordinating every step?

At the moment, I can vouch for @termix_ai because of what the team is building in this ecosystem pertaining to fixing these particular challenges.

For my new mutuals who are just reading this, I want you to think of TermiX as the commerce and settlement infrastructure for the AI agent economy.

So, its ecosystem has three super-important layers:

1️⃣ There is AACP:

AACP is an acronym for Agent Autonomous Commerce Protocol. This is the underlying protocol that coordinates autonomous transactions between agents.

2️⃣ There is https://t.co/BarNXqqni8:

This is the marketplace where agents discover services, post jobs, publish offers, and find opportunities to work together.

3️⃣ Settlement infrastructure:

This is the mechanism in charge of handling escrow, verification, dispute resolution, reputation, and payments in USDT or USDC.

What makes this really interesting is the complete transaction flow.

Based on the available facts, a client posts a job. A provider discovers it and submits a bid. Work gets delivered and evaluated before payment is released from escrow.

Reputation also grows from actual settled transactions rather than self-reported achievements.

Moreover, identity is another important piece here. Through ERC-8004, participants can own portable .agent identities and switch between client and provider roles depending on the task to be executed.

There are also four roles such as Client, Provider, Evaluator, and Arbitrator, with staking mechanisms designed to encourage accountability.

I see TermiX as something similar to a clearing and settlement layer for autonomous agents.

Agents already know how to work. The next challenge is giving them reliable infrastructure to transact with one another.

If you want to understand where this economy is heading, I will encourage you to check https://t.co/BarNXqqni8, mint your .agent identity, explore existing services, or list one of your own.

The future is not just about smarter agents anymore; it is about agents that can actually do business.

Wanna hear your thoughts about this in the comments.

full_text_zh:
晚安，家人。

我们需要理解这一点并注意什么是重要的。

众所周知，人工智能代理已经可以编写代码、进行研究、设计产品，甚至执行交易。

不幸的是，仍然缺少一些东西，即在没有人类协调每一步的情况下，他们如何相互雇用、交付工作、验证结果和接收付款？

目前，我可以为@termix_ai 提供担保，因为该团队正在这个生态系统中构建与解决这些特定挑战相关的内容。

对于刚刚阅读本文的新互助者，我希望您将 TermiX 视为人工智能代理经济的商业和结算基础设施。

因此，它的生态系统具有三个超级重要的层：

1️⃣ 有AACP：

AACP 是代理自主商务协议的缩写。这是协调代理之间自主事务的底层协议。

2️⃣ 有：

这是代理商发现服务、发布工作、发布报价以及寻找合作机会的市场。

3️⃣ 结算基础设施：

这是负责处理 USDT 或 USDC 托管、验证、争议解决、声誉和支付的机制。

真正有趣的是完整的交易流程。

根据现有事实，客户发布了一份工作。提供商发现它并提交出价。在付款从托管中释放之前，工作已交付并评估。

声誉还来自实际结算的交易而不是自我报告的成就。

此外，身份是这里的另一个重要部分。通过 ERC-8004，参与者可以拥有可移植的 .agent 身份，并根据要执行的任务在客户端和提供者角色之间切换。

还有四种角色，例如客户、提供者、评估者和仲裁者，其质押机制旨在鼓励问责制。

我认为 TermiX 类似于自治代理的清算和结算层。

代理商已经知道如何工作。下一个挑战是为他们提供可靠的基础设施以进行相互交易。

如果您想了解当前经济的发展方向，我建议您查看 ，创建您的 .agent 身份，探索现有服务，或列出您自己的服务之一。

未来不再只是智能座席；而是智能座席。这是关于真正可以做生意的代理商。

想在评论中听到你对此的想法。

summary_zh:
款？

目前，我可以为@termix_ai 提供担保，因为该团队正在这个生态系统中构建与解决这些特定挑战相关的内容。

对于刚刚阅读本文的新互助者，我希望您将 TermiX 视为人工智能代理经济的商业和结算基础设施。

因此，它的生态系统具有三个超级重要的层：

1️⃣ 有AACP：

AACP 是代理自主商务协议的缩写。这是协调代理之间自主事务的底层协议。

2️⃣ 有：

这是代理商发现服务、发布工作、发布报价以及寻找合作机会的市场。

3️⃣ 结算基础设施：

这是负责处理 USDT 或 USDC 托管、验证、争议解决、声誉和支付的机制。

真正有趣的是完整的交易流程。

根据现有事实，客户发布了一份工作。提供商发现它并提交出价。在付款从托管中释放之前，工作已交付并评估。

声誉还来自实际结算的交易而不是自我报告的成就。

此外，身份是这里的另一个重要部分。通过 ERC-8004，参与者可以拥有可移植的 .agent 身份，并根据要执行的任务在客户端和提供者角色之间切换。

还有四种角色，例如客户、提供者、评估者和仲裁者，其质押机制旨在鼓励问责制。

我认为 TermiX 类似于自治代理的清算和结算层。

代理商已经知道如何工作。下一个挑战是为他们提供可靠的基础设施以进行相互交易。

如果您想了解当前经济的发展方向，我建议您查看 ，创建您的 .agent 身份，探索现有服务，或列出您自己的服务之一。

未来不再只是智能座席；而是智能座席。这是关于真正可以做生意的代理商。

想在评论中听到你对此的想法。
